chunks: And as for what Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Abd al-Ghaffar al-Jazi who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj/Umrah) who is compelled to eat carrion (meat of an animal that died naturally), and he finds it, and also finds game (freshly killed or alive). He said: He eats the carrion and leaves the game. The meaning in this report is one of two things: One is that it is to be attributed to a form of taqiyya (dissimulation/prudence), because that is the view of some of the Sunnis. And the second is that it is directed to one who finds the game not yet slaughtered (or alive), for he eats the carrion and frees the game (lets it go). And we said this because when the person in ihram slaughters the game, its ruling is the ruling of the carrion. And if it is so, and he finds the carrion, he should restrict himself to it and not slaughter the living animal, but rather let it go.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةُ: Dissimulation or prudence in religious practice
key_terms.الْمَيْتَةُ: Carrion (meat of an animal that died naturally)
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: Person in ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What should a pilgrim in ihram eat if compelled: carrion or fresh game?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi presents two primary juristic interpretations for this ruling: either it reflects *taqiyya* to align with Sunni views that prohibit eating game while in *ihram*, or it addresses a specific scenario where the pilgrim consumes carrion to avoid slaughting the live animal, thereby preserving its status as distinct from *meitah*. This highlights the nuanced Shia approach to resolving apparent contradictions between general prohibitions and specific necessities during pilgrimage.
